newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bundesbank says German rate cut a clear signal.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank says German rate cut a clear signal.

text.p: Otmar Issing, the Bundesbank chief economist, said the German central bank's last cut in its key money market or repo rate on August 22 sent a clear signal to financial markets.
Noting that the cut to 3.00 percent from 3.30 percent was "clearly more than many had expected", he said the current repo rate had now reached an "all-time low".

Reiterating comments by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, Issing told a financial seminar in Zurich that he once more wanted to make clear that the Bundesbank had sent a signal with its larger-than-expected cut.
"We have created clarity for the foreseeable future," he said, echoing views Tietmeyer's had expressed.
"With this clear step we are signalling that the level has been reached."
He said slowing money supply growth allowed the Bundesbank to take this step.
He added that addressing Germany's 10 percent unemployment problem and reforming its cumbersome tax system was now in the hands of politicians in Bonn, not something for the Bundesbank.
Issing noted Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) clearly improved in the second quarter of 1996 compared with the first quarter.
"The second quarter should come out clearly better than the first. That was to be expected," he said in answer to a question after a speech to bankers in Zurich.
Germany will report its second quarter GDP on Thursday.

German GDP fell by 0.5 percent in the first quarter of this year from the fourth quarter of 1995. The Federal Satistics Office revised the fourth quarter figure to unchanged from a fall of 0.5 percent reported previously.
GDP in the first quarter was 0.3 percent higher than in the same quarter a year earlier.
